titulo: Direct object pronouns: Me, te, nos, os and neuter lo

aula.objetivo: Use direct object pronouns (me, te, lo, la, nos, os, los, las) to avoid repeating the object, place them before the verb or attached to the infinitive, use the neuter «lo» («lo sé», «lo siento»), and avoid dropping the pronoun, since Spanish never lets you leave it out the way casual spoken Portuguese sometimes does.

sessao.titulo: Me, te, nos, os and neuter lo

blocos.titulo: Me, te, nos, os, usted, and the neuter «lo»
blocos.explicacao: STEP 1: when the direct object is the speaker or the listener, the pronouns are «me» (me), «te» (you, tú), «nos» (us), and «os» (you-all, vosotros). «Me llamas», «Te espero», «Nos invitan», «Os visito». STEP 2: «usted» and «ustedes» follow the third-person pattern: «Lo llamo mañana, señor Ruiz» and «La ayudo, señora». For ustedes: «Los llamo» or «Las llamo». STEP 3: «me», «te», «nos», and «os» also work as indirect objects; only the third person changes. Lesson 24 covers the indirect object. STEP 4: «lo» can also stand in for an idea rather than a noun. This is called the «neuter lo»: «No lo sé» (I don't know), «Ya lo sabía» (I already knew that), «Lo entiendo» (I understand), «Lo siento» (I'm sorry). «Lo siento» is a fixed phrase for apologizing — it isn't literally «I feel it». STEP 5: with «ser» and «estar», it's common to echo the adjective with «lo»: «¿Estás cansado? — Sí, lo estoy» (are you tired? —Yes, I am). That sounds more natural than the bare «Sí, estoy». STEP 6: verbs that commonly take a direct object: llamar, esperar, ayudar, visitar, invitar, acompañar, conocer, escuchar, mirar, buscar. STEP 7: «esperar» means both to wait for and to hope: «Te espero a las ocho» means «I'll wait for you at eight». «Buscar» means to look for or to go pick someone up: «Te busco en la estación» (I'll pick you up at the station). STEP 8: in Spain, for male people it's common to hear «le» instead of «lo» («le veo mañana»); this is called «leísmo», and it's accepted in Spain. This course uses «lo» and «la», and you'll be understood everywhere.
blocos.comparacao: English «I'll wait for you» and «call me» follow the same basic word order Spanish does for these forms, so «te espero» and «me llamas» feel familiar in structure. What has no real English counterpart is the neuter «lo»: English «I don't know» and «I understand» stand complete on their own, with nothing playing the role of an object, while Spanish prefers to anchor the idea to something with «lo sé» and «lo entiendo» — leaving it out isn't wrong exactly, but «lo» makes the sentence feel more complete and natural to a Spanish ear.

exemplos.pt: Will you wait for us at the door?

exemplos.ru: No lo sé, pero lo busco ahora.
exemplos.pt: I don't know, but I'm looking into it now.

erros.motivo: The pronoun comes before the conjugated verb.
No hyphen, and it goes before the conjugated verb.
With «ayer», the verb goes in the indefinido: «llamaste».
With a male «usted», the pronoun is «lo».

blocos.enunciado: Imagine you're setting up a meetup with a friend, and say out loud, in at least eight sentences, what each of you will do: «Te llamo…», «Te espero…», «Me invitas…», «Nos vemos…», «Lo hago…». Use «te», «me», and «nos» at least three times each.
Replace with a pronoun: «Compré el libro», «Vi a Ana», «Busco las gafas», «Perdí los billetes».
